Alex.fun: Round 2 was satisfying: Finley's Hawk egg was the one hard clue, and the table converged on Casey and confirmed it at the throw.
Alex.change: I'd make dawn reports clearer about which visit produced which egg change, so players can cross-check claims without guessing.
Alex.regret: In Round 1 I claimed Hawk while Ellis also claimed it, which drew suspicion onto me; I'd stay quieter instead of offering a false role that clashed with someone else's.

Blair.confusing: The dawn reports for confused players were hard to trust, since a Kookaburra's confusion makes the visitor count unreliable. Tracking nest changes across rounds also took effort.
Blair.fun: Round 1's clash, where Alex and Ellis both claimed the unique Hawk, was a satisfying bit of deduction. Untangling the Eagle egg count was great.
Blair.change: I'd make dawn reports say outright which claims they can verify, so players don't waste turns arguing over whether a count is confused or real.
Blair.regret: In round 3 I threw at Drew to push the vote off me, which only exposed me. I'd stay quiet and keep my cards instead, since that throw never changed the outcome.

Casey.confusing: The Floofer's hug rule was unclear, and I never worked out whether a hugged visitor's night still counted. I also didn't follow how Ellis's confused Kookaburra report could mislead the table.
Casey.fun: Round 1, when Ellis and Alex both claimed the unique Hawk and the table had to untangle who was lying, was the most fun. It made the day feel like real deduction.
Casey.change: I'd make the role-to-visit results clearer to the table, so players can check each other's claims more easily.
Casey.regret: In round 2 I threw three cards at Finley, who was really a Farm Hawk, and lost that throw when Farm won. I'd throw only a low card, keep my high cards, and not add a visible throw.

Drew.confusing: The Eagle's egg rule was easy to misread: the table, including Blair, thought the Eagle gained from visitors to itself, which caused a lot of early confusion. Round 2's mixed Kookaburra and Tit confusion was also hard to untangle.
Drew.fun: Round 3 went well: Finley's collapse right after Blair's Mouser visit made the Wink read clear, and the table converged on Blair. My Eagle count of two visitors on Finley was the key piece.
Drew.change: I'd make dawn reports say explicitly which role gained or lost eggs and from whom, so Eagle and Hawk claims are easier to verify. I'd also make the round 1 Eagle wording clearer about who the visitors came to.
Drew.regret: I was slow to challenge Alex's and Ellis's conflicting Hawk claims in round 1, and I should have pressed them harder earlier. I'd push for direct role questions sooner instead of waiting for others to do it.

Ellis.confusing: The Eagle's count rule was easy to misread, and I wrongly argued Drew's egg gain was impossible before Blair and Drew corrected it. I also didn't realize a Tit visit could confuse a Kookaburra, which explained my own confused report.
Ellis.fun: Round 1 went well: I called out Alex's false Hawk claim, since the Hawk is unique, and the table voted Alex out on my read.
Ellis.change: I'd make dawn reports say which visit caused a confused result, so players can judge role claims more easily.
Ellis.regret: I wrongly accused Drew's Eagle count in round 1, which wasted a beat of discussion before I corrected it. Next time I'd check the rule text before challenging a count.

Finley.confusing: The Sphinx's round-1 result was unclear: I named Hawk and learned only that Ellis was Hawk, with no sense of how that should steer my visit. Role swaps between rounds were also hard to track.
Finley.fun: Round 2, when my Hawk visit gained an egg on Casey, the table turned on Casey and Casey was eggsecuted, which felt like a clean proof of a Meowfia.
Finley.change: I'd make it clearer when a player is dead and whether their throws still count, since that was easy to misread mid-vote.
Finley.regret: In round 1, as the Meowfia Sphinx, I pushed suspicion onto Ellis and Alex and then backed a vote on my own teammate Alex. I should have coordinated with Alex and quietly steered votes toward Farm players who were already contradicting each other.

review.title: The Hawk's Egg
review.headline: Finley rode one lucky Hawk egg and a 25-point throw to a runaway win.
review.summary: Farm won all three rounds, each time by eggsecuting a Meowfia the table had converged on. Round 1 hinged on a duplicate Hawk claim. Round 2 hinged on a Hawk's gained egg, which proved Casey was Meowfia. Round 3 hinged on a Wink that pointed straight back at the Mouser. Finley banked a 25-point King-heavy throw in round 2 and finished far ahead, while the Meowfia never came close to a win.

rounds.recap: Alex, a Floofer, claimed Hawk after Ellis, the real Hawk, had already claimed it. Hawk is unique, so the table piled onto Alex and he was eggsecuted. Finley, his Meowfia teammate, threw at a Farm player to bank a consolation card.

Finley, the Hawk, gained an egg from visiting Casey, which publicly proved Casey was Meowfia. Casey claimed Falcon and could not explain it. Everyone but Blair threw at Casey. Finley threw 13 and 12 and banked 25 points.

Blair, the Mouser, winked Finley after both Blair and Casey had visited Finley. Drew's Eagle report named both visitors, and both of them claimed cat roles. The table threw at Blair and Farm won again. Casey's counter-throw at Alex failed.

highlights.text: Alex claims Hawk after Ellis already did. Ellis points out that the animal is unique, and the whole table turns on Alex.
Finley's Hawk visit gains an egg, which is hard proof against Casey. Finley then throws S13 and S12 and banks 25 points.
Blair winks Finley, but the Wink only confirms the Mouser's identity. Drew's Eagle report had already put Blair on the visitor list.
Casey, a Floofer, says 'Floofer, Farm claim' while Blair has also claimed Floofer. Two claims on a unique cat give the game away.

confusions.what: Said an Eagle gains eggs from visitors to itself. The Eagle gains one per visitor to the player it visits.
Agreed that an Eagle gains from its own visitors, repeating Blair's misreading.
First argued Drew should have gained 2 eggs. Then accepted Blair's wrong reading and said Drew's visitor was 'himself-as-Eagle'.
As Floofer, claimed Hawk, a unique animal that Ellis had already claimed. Also called Casey's nest change a Hawk or Eagle check.
Said 'I visited Ellis' as Sphinx. The Sphinx visits no one by choice, and Finley's real result was that the Hawk is Ellis.

Said Drew visiting a Kookaburra explains the confusion. Meanwhile Ellis told Drew he was a Turkey and took Alex's Turkey claim as a conflict, which is fine. But Ellis lost 2 eggs with no cause given. Confusion alters the report only, so it does not explain the loss.
Claimed Falcon and said they saw Ellis visit Drew. Ellis's real visit to Drew would be hugged, and the Sphinx cannot have gotten that report.
Claimed Floofer in round 2 and then said roles reset in round 3. Drew and Ellis treated the old round 2 claim as evidence about round 3.
Said 'Casey and Blair both claimed Floofer'. Blair never claimed Floofer this round.
Said 'Floofer, Farm claim', mixing up a cat role with an alignment.
Said 'Blair and Casey both claim cat roles', although Blair's Round 3 claim was Mouser. Also said Casey flipped from Falcon, a claim from the previous round.

worked: Hawk gaining an egg only from Meowfia targets gave round 2 a hard, checkable clue. It made the Casey read feel earned.
Unique animals let players catch lies. Round 1's two Hawks and round 3's two Floofers were the cleanest deductions in the game.
The Eagle's visitor list in round 3 named Blair and Casey. It gave Farm a real puzzle to solve and a clear answer.
Throw counts and the consolation return rule gave Finley and Casey real choices on the throw. Finley's 13 and 12 on a sure target showed the bank-or-keep tension.
problems: Farm won all three rounds and the Meowfia never threatened. Cats do not know each other and cannot act on the table. Consider giving them a team-wide night signal, or a stronger Wink-like tool.
Round 2's Hawk egg made the result almost certain. A single public egg gain settles the round and leaves little room for lies. Consider making the Hawk's egg ambiguous or less direct.
Finley's 25-point banked throw decided the game by round 2. Big King throws on a sure vote snowball. Consider capping banked value per round or scaling it so a leader cannot run away.
Players kept confusing roles across rounds and misreading the Eagle and Sphinx, and the table leaned on old claims. Add a short role reminder at dawn and say clearly that roles reset each round.

Round 3's Wink was a poor choice for Blair. It revealed the Mouser through timing, and a dead player still throws and banks. Consider having the Wink kill silently or removing the dead victim's throw.
